newsitem.title: USA: Former Baron stockbroker pleads guilty.
newsitem.headline: Former Baron stockbroker pleads guilty.

text.p: A key stockbroker at a defunct investment firm who made $4.7 million by cheating investors pleaded guilty Thursday to racketeering charges and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors.

The broker, Roman Okin, 29, had worked for the now-defunct investment firm of A.R. Baron & Co. Last month, Okin, a Russian immigrant, and 12 other brokers were charged with lying to investors, manipulating market prices and making unauthorised trades.
Prosecutors have described Okin as the No. 2 man in the firm. Among the charges in the 174-count indictment is that he sold stocks to industrialists in England.
Okin pleaded guilty to one count of enterprise corruption in state court. He faces up to 25 years in prison.

But the prosecutor told Judge Edward McLaughin that at a sentencing hearing in September he would detail how Okin cooperated with authorities, and indicated Okin could get one to three years in prison.
Prosecutors alleged Okin made $4.7 million during a two-year period by cheating investors.
On Monday, two other brokers, Garvey Fox, 29, and Matthew Hirsch, 30, also pleaded guilty to participating in a criminal enterpise and agreed to cooperate.
"Okin was Baron's best salesman," Assistant District Attorney John Moscow said after the hearing. "He is charged with more counts, 79, in the indictment than anyone else. He was the most productive."
Moscow said Okin blew his money in gambling sprees and would spend thousands of dollars a night at strip clubs and restaurants.
Baron had about 8,000 investors when it was shut down by regulators last July. The firm is accused of cheating investors out of more than $75 million.

Among the victims of the alleged swindle are New York University, which lost more than $600,000; Anthony Pilkington of Manchester, England, whose family owns a huge glass-making company and who was bilked out of at least $500,000; and Hong Kong businessman Keith Hsu, who lost more than $1 million, prosecutors said.

The remaining 10 defendants include former Baron President Andrew Bressman. He is accused of funnelling investors' money into his own accounts to finance visits to strip clubs and buying luxury cars, prosecutors said.

Because Baron cleared its trades through the brokerage Bear Stearns, unsuspecting clients figured their investments were in secure hands, authorities said. Prosecutors would not say whether Bear Stearns was part of an ongoing investigation.
Assistant District Attorney Moscow said prosecutors were looking into reports that Bear Stearns may have destroyed documents related to the Baron firm.
